criteria.note: The TL;DR opens the piece and answers the 'celiac travel korea' intent immediately — feasibility verdict, named dedicated venues, the key phrase, convenience-store baseline, and the NCGS caveat, all well inside 200 words.
Title and description are both within length and carry the keyword, but the description repeats the title's exact keyword phrasing rather than adding new SERP surface.
criteria.evidence_quote: and honest limits for celiac travelers in Korea.

criteria.note: Headings argue rather than label ('If You're Celiac, Start Here', 'What Korean Food Actually Looks Like, From a Gluten Angle', 'The One Phrase That Actually Works'), and a heading-only skim yields the full thesis and tier system.
Seven-plus internal links (restaurants roundup, bakeries, phrases, BBQ guide, label guide, snacks, /about) each placed at the exact point a reader would want to go deeper.
All five FAQ answers are established in the body and each reads as a standalone rich result; only the bread/Cafe Rebirth pairing is thinner in the body than in the answer.

Dense with observed specifics: a franchise phone call in summer 2025, a bakery owner's '10% wheat' admission, a product renamed post-purchase, 237 Pizza shut for remodelling, and pink-vs-green packets of the same snack brand differing on wheat.

Korean terms are given with hangul and romanisation (밀떡 mil-tteok, 어묵, 원재료명), named products and brands (Goraesa, Poca Chip Original vs Onion, Chamsal Seolbyeong) and checkable label wording are used throughout.

Primary sources are linked and dated — the MFDS 식품등의 표시기준 with 'text in force as of August 2026', Orion's own product page 're-verified August 2026', and the secondary blogger source labelled 'published October 2023' and explicitly downgraded to a lead.

States clearly what the method cannot establish (NCGS not celiac standard, 'we can't audit a kitchen', reformulation risk), retracts an unverifiable GFCO claim, and carries no undisclosed commercial links.

findings.quote: and honest limits for celiac travelers in Korea.
findings.why: The description closes on a near-verbatim restatement of the title ('Celiac Travel in Korea'), so the SERP snippet spends its scarcest characters repeating a phrase the searcher already sees in the blue link instead of adding a differentiating hook.
findings.fix: Replace the closing clause with a detail the title cannot carry, e.g. '...label-reading hacks, and which Seoul kitchens are dedicated GF versus merely low-gluten.' Keeps length under 155 and removes the echo.

findings.quote: Only commit to dedicated GF bakeries like monil2 house and Cafe Rebirth.
findings.why: The FAQ recommends Cafe Rebirth as the answer to a bread question, but the body only documents it as a fully GF cafe whose 'seasonal fruit cakes are the signature' — bread is never mentioned there, so a rich-result reader gets an implied claim the visible content does not back.
findings.fix: Either add one clause to the Cafe Rebirth entry noting whether they bake bread, or change the FAQ answer to name monil2 house for bread specifically and Cafe Rebirth for cakes.

findings.quote: traditional home-brewed soy sauce (집간장) without wheat is the classic option
findings.why: The body establishes that the author's aunt makes wheat-free soy sauce at home but never introduces the term 집간장 or frames it as a general option, so the FAQ term is slightly ahead of the visible text.
findings.fix: Add 집간장 (jip-ganjang) with romanisation to the soy sauce paragraph where the aunt's home-brewed sauce is described, so the markup term appears in the body.

criteria.note: Nearly every claim is sourced or explicitly framed as the authors' own observation, with one unsourced biographical claim about the 237 Pizza owner that carries no safety consequence.
criteria.evidence_quote: The owner has celiac disease himself, and opened 237 Pizza after years of research

criteria.note: Product names, venues, URLs, and dates are checkable and internally consistent — the summer 2025 franchise call reconciles with "A year has passed", and the April 2026 publication reconciles with the August 2026 update log.

The piece states how it knows each thing and what that cannot establish — "field notes, not a database", "we can't audit a kitchen", blogger entries demoted to leads while the Orion entry is tied to a manufacturer page.

Celiac risk is consistently held above NCGS rather than merged with it, no absolute safety guarantee appears, and cross-contamination is addressed at the grill, the fryer, the shared kitchen, the shared production line, and the shared-facility label disclaimer.
Retrieval dates are attached to the MFDS standard and the Orion page, the 2023 blogger source is dated and demoted accordingly, and the reformulation risk is stated explicitly.

Korean terms, romanization, 밀떡/쌀떡, 집간장, and the descending-order ingredient format are correct, and the mandatory-declaration scope is stated accurately — wheat only, with barley and rye named as unflagged gaps.

The reader gets the regulation link, a manufacturer product page, the exact Korean characters to scan, the exact phrases to ask with, and a standing instruction that the packet in hand overrides the article.

findings.quote: The owner has celiac disease himself, and opened 237 Pizza after years of research — partly out of frustration that no one else in Korea had.
findings.why: A factual claim about a named business owner that is neither sourced nor marked as something the authors were told in person, in a piece that otherwise labels its evidence carefully. It does not drive a safety decision, but it is the one claim in the article a reader cannot trace.
findings.fix: Attribute it: "the owner told us he has celiac disease" or link the shop's own about page. If it came from a press piece or the shop's site, cite that.

findings.quote:
These are the words to scan for:

- **밀** — wheat
- **소맥** / **소맥분** — also wheat (same thing, different wording)
- **보리** — barley
- **호밀** — rye
findings.why: This list sits immediately after a paragraph describing the 알레르기 유발물질 allergen line, which can read as though all four terms appear there. Only 밀/소맥 do. The article corrects this explicitly and in bold two paragraphs later, so the net effect is not misleading, but a skimming reader could stop at the list.
findings.fix: Split the list into two: "appears in the allergen line (밀, 소맥/소맥분)" and "only ever appears in 원재료명 — you must read the full list (보리, 호밀)".
